profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This is the Green Data Center, a research computing facility on Syracuse University campus in Syracuse, New York, completed in 2009 in partnership with IBM. The facility was among the first university data centers designed around on site trigeneration, using natural gas microturbines to generate electricity on site, with the resulting waste heat captured for both heating and, through absorption chillers, cooling, an approach intended to reduce reliance on the regional power grid and improve energy efficiency versus a conventional data center. The project drew industry and trade press attention at the time, including coverage in Campus Technology and Cabling Installation and Maintenance, as an early example of a university investing in sustainable data center design. Syracuse University own research computing division continues to describe the Green Data Center as central to the university high performance and research computing capacity. No specific critical IT megawattage figure was found published on the university own site. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project.

reading.body:
SU Green Data Center is a research computing facility on Syracuse University's campus completed in 2009 in partnership with IBM. The facility's IT capacity in megawatts is not published, so its contribution to the state's data center stock cannot be measured against the one facility in New York with a public specification. The university describes it as central to its high performance and research computing operations.

The facility was designed around on-site trigeneration using natural gas microturbines to generate electricity with waste heat captured for heating and cooling, reducing dependence on the regional power grid. This approach was novel for university data centers at its completion. Whether this efficiency advantage persists, or whether the facility's reliance on on-site generation rather than grid supply constrains its scaling potential, depends on facts not published.

Thirty-one data center facilities are mapped in New York, but only one besides this one publishes IT megawattage. Without a published figure for SU Green Data Center, its role in the state's AI compute footprint cannot be assessed. The facility's research mission and on-campus location suggest it serves university workloads rather than commercial AI training, but this is not stated in the specifications available.
